newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seen managing 1997 budget meeting EMU test.
newsitem.headline: Spain seen managing 1997 budget meeting EMU test.

text.p: Spain will present a 1997 budget to parliament next week that will slash 1.2 trillion pesetas ($9.41 billion) from the public deficit and whip the country into shape for a European single currency -- at least on paper.
The minority Popular Party government expects to gain cabinet approval for the draft on Friday and will present the budget to parliament next Monday.
It has pledged to deliver an austere package that will cut the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from a projected 4.4 percent in 1996.
The government is counting on a rise in receipts of six percent, while expenditure growth will be capped at two percent, 0.6 percentage points below the inflation rate forecast for 1997.
Even so, it must find another 800 billion pesetas in cuts or put at risk its European aspirations by missing the Maastricht test for joining a single currency.
"Spain will meet the criteria somehow, someway," a senior government official said privately.
The government's optimism is based on an expected pick-up in domestic Spanish growth in 1997, as well as hopes for the economic revival of its neighbours.
The government plans to freeze public salaries, cut 10 percent off current expenditures and impose a new four percent levy on non-life insurance.

Cutting funds to the public sector and gaining income from privatisation should also pump up central government receipts, while the drain from unemployment subsidies should be staunched by the economic recovery.
The government is also tackling inflation decisively, containing tariff rises in the crucial rate-regulated sectors to less than the projected inflation rate.
Still, analysts fear the government has staked its goals on forecasts that could go awry.
"The budget has a lot of good intentions, but if their forecasts are not correct they will end up needing additional measures," one analyst said.
They also worry the administration will lack the muscle to implement the cuts, especially the most unpopular ones.
"On paper it is relatively easy to draw up a tight budget. What is difficult is to accomplish it," a dealer said.
Their task has also been made more difficult by a surprise gap of 721 billion pesetas in 1995 accounts inherited from the former Socialist government that was unearthed over the summer.
The gap forced Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato to set the 1995 budget deficit to gross domestic product ratio at 6.6 percent, up from the previous forecast of 5.8 percent.
Despite the tough budget proposals, the government should nonetheless have little difficulty shepherding the measures through parliament.
It appears to have resolved differences over health spending and taxation with its nationalist allies and therefore should be able to count on the backing of a clear majority. ($1=127.5 Peseta)
